An arithmetic function f is multiplicative if f(mn)=f(m)f(n) whenever m and n are coprime integers. If g(n)=∑d∣n​f(d) and (m,n)=1, every positive integer divisor of mn is uniquely d1​d2​ with d1​∣m and d2​∣n. Hence
g(mn)=∑d1​∣m​∑d2​∣n​f(d1​d2​)=(∑d1​∣m​f(d1​))(∑d2​∣n​f(d2​))=g(m)g(n),
(1)
so g is multiplicative.
The Möbius function is defined by μ(1)=1, μ(n)=0 if the square of a prime number divides n, and μ(n)=(−1)r if n is a product of r distinct prime numbers. Coprime integers have disjoint sets of prime factors, so this definition immediately gives μ(mn)=μ(m)μ(n) when (m,n)=1.
For n=p1a1​​⋯prar​​>1, only the square-free divisors contribute, and therefore
∑d∣n​μ(d)=∏j=1r​(1−1)=0.
(2)
For n=1 the sum is 1. Thus 1∗μ=ε in the language of Dirichlet convolution. Convolving g=1∗f with μ gives the Möbius inversion formula
f(n)=(μ∗g)(n)=∑e∣n​μ(e)g(n/e).
(3)
If f(n)=n, its divisor sum is the sum-of-divisors function. Conversely, if g(n)=n, Möbius inversion gives
f(n)=∑e∣n​μ(e)en​=φ(n),
(4)
using the standard divisor identity for the Euler totient function. Therefore the two requested answers are
g(n)=σ1​(n),f(n)=φ(n).​
(5)

2F OurBigBook.com
One form of the Baire category theorem says that a nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets.
For each nonnegative integer n, put
Zn​={z∈C:f(n)(z)=0}.
(6)
Because f is an entire function, every derivative f(n) is continuous and Zn​ is closed. No f(n) is identically zero: if f(n)≡0 for some n, repeated integration shows that f is a polynomial. By the identity theorem, the zero set of the nonzero holomorphic function f(n) has empty interior. Thus each Zn​ is nowhere dense.
The complex plane is complete, so the Baire category theorem gives
C=⋃n=0∞​Zn​.
(7)
Choose z0​ outside this union. Then f(n)(z0​)=0 for every n, and hence every coefficient f(n)(z0​)/n! in the Taylor series about z0​ is nonzero. Such a point z0​ therefore exists.

The relation g(X)h(X)=X7−1 makes this a length-seven binary cyclic code. Since degg=3, the generator polynomial of a cyclic code gives
dimC=7−degg=4.
(8)
The polynomial g itself is a codeword of Hamming weight three, so the minimum distance is at most three. A nonzero word of weight one cannot vanish at the nonzero element α. If a weight-two word Xi+Xj vanished there, then αi−j=1; because α has order seven and 0≤i,j<7, this forces i=j. Hence there are no nonzero words of weight below three, and
rankC=4,d(C)=3.​
(9)
The equation g(α)=0 gives α3=α2+1 in the finite field F8​, and therefore
α4=α(α2+1)=α3+α=α2+α+1=r(α).
(10)
By the root-evaluation syndrome for a cyclic code, this is the syndrome of the single error e(X)=X4. Since d(C)=3, minimum-distance decoding uniquely corrects one error. Subtracting and adding agree over F2​, so the decoded codeword is
c(X)=r(X)+X4=X4+X2+X+1=(X+1)g(X).​
(11)

A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form when every production rule has one of the forms
A→BC,A→a,
(12)
where A,B,C are nonterminal symbols and a is a terminal symbol. If the language contains the empty word, one may additionally permit S0​→ϵ, with the start symbol S0​ absent from all right-hand sides.

b

Words: 129 Articles: 1
4G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 129
b OurBigBook.com
The standard conversion of a context-free grammar to Chomsky normal form proceeds as follows:
Add a fresh start symbol S0​ with S0​→S.
Find the nullable nonterminals, add the variants obtained by omitting nullable occurrences, and remove all epsilon productions. Omit S0​→ϵ as well because the requested language excludes ϵ.
Remove every unit production A→B by copying the non-unit productions reachable from B to A.
Remove nonterminals that are unreachable from S0​ or cannot derive a terminal word.
In every right-hand side of length at least two, replace a terminal a by a fresh nonterminal Ta​ with Ta​→a.
Replace each right-hand side of length greater than two by a chain of binary productions using fresh nonterminals.
Each remaining production is of the required binary or terminal form, and these transformations preserve every nonempty generated word. Thus L(GChom​)=L(G)∖{ϵ}.

L(G)={anbcn:n≥0},
(13)
because each use of S→ASc adds one a on the left and one c on the right, and S→B→b terminates the derivation.
Introduce nonterminals S0​,X,C and use
S0​SXAC​→AX∣b,→AX∣b,→SC,→a,→c.​
(14)
Every production is in Chomsky normal form. The production X→SC completes one matched a,c pair, while either start-like symbol terminates with b, so the grammar generates exactly the same language. These productions are a valid GChom​.

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 188 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 188
5J OurBigBook.com
Treat the cell counts as independent Poisson random variables. Under independence of Month and Hospital, the independence log-linear model for a two-way contingency table is
logμij​=λ+αi​+βj​,
(15)
with no Month–Hospital interaction. Compare its Poisson deviance with the appropriate upper quantile of a chi-squared distribution. This is the likelihood-ratio test of independence in a contingency table.
The approximation assumes independent counts with correctly specified Poisson means, identifiable parameters, and sufficiently large fitted cell means for the asymptotic chi-squared law to be accurate. Equivalently, one may condition on the margins and use the corresponding multinomial sampling formulation.
For the 12×3 month table there are 36 cells and 1+11+2=14 independent model parameters, so the residual degrees of freedom are
(12−1)(3−1)=22.
(16)
Since
28.51836<χ22,0.992​=40.29,
(17)
model 1 does not reject Month–Hospital independence at the 1% level.
After combining months into four quarters, the table is 4×3, giving
(4−1)(3−1)=6
(18)
degrees of freedom. Now
17.9181>χ6,0.992​=16.81,
(19)
so model 2 rejects Quarter–Hospital independence at the 1% level.
There is no contradiction. Relabelling twelve months as four quarters aggregates the contingency table, changes the null hypothesis, and reduces the degrees of freedom. The quarter-level hospital pattern is coherent enough to cross the much lower six-degree-of-freedom threshold even though the more detailed month-level omnibus test does not. This is an instance of how aggregation can change a contingency-table independence test.

F(z)=z−a​z+a​

so that F(z)∼z as z→∞. This branch cut gives, for −a<x<a, the boundary values
F+​(x)=ia2−x2​,F−​(x)=−ia2−x2​.

Integrate F over the boundary of a large disk with a thin slit removed. The upper bank is traversed from −a to a and the lower bank from a to −a, so together they contribute
2i∫−aa​a2−x2​dx.

F(z)=z(1−z2a2​)1/2=z−2za2​+O(z−3),

−πia2+2i∫−aa​a2−x2​dx=0,
(34)

∫−aa​a2−x2​dx=2πa2​.​

Write an integral binary quadratic form as [a,b,c]=ax2+bxy+cy2, with discriminant of a binary quadratic form D=b2−4ac. It is positive definite when a>0 and D<0. Two forms are equivalent if one is obtained from the other by an integral linear change of variables whose matrix lies in SL2​(Z). A positive definite form is reduced when
∣b∣≤a≤c,
(51)
with b≥0 when ∣b∣=a or a=c.
To reduce a form, apply a unimodular shear x↦x+ny with n chosen so that the new middle coefficient has ∣b′∣≤a. If the new final coefficient c′ is smaller than a, exchange the variables, using a determinant-one rotation, so that the positive leading coefficient decreases from a to c′. Repeating must stop because a positive integer cannot decrease indefinitely. At termination ∣b∣≤a≤c, and elementary sign changes impose the boundary convention. This is the reduction algorithm for a positive definite binary quadratic form, and proves that every positive definite form is equivalent to a reduced one.
The displayed forms have discriminant 1−36=−35, so the intended discriminant is −35. For any reduced form of this discriminant, enumeration of reduced binary quadratic forms gives
1≤a≤335​​<4,∣b∣≤a,c=4ab2+35​∈Z.
(52)
The boundary convention and direct checking of a=1,2,3 leave only
f1​=[1,1,9]=x2+xy+9y2,f2​=[3,1,3]=3x2+xy+3y2.​
(53)
Suppose first that a prime p>7 is represented by f1​. The identity
4f1​(x,y)=(2x+y)2+35y2
(54)
shows modulo both 5 and 7 that 4p is a nonzero square. Hence
(5p​)=(7p​)=1.
(55)
Similarly,
12f2​(x,y)=(6x+y)2+35y2.
(56)
Modulo 5, this says 2p is a square, while modulo 7 it says 5p is a square. Since (2/5)=(5/7)=−1, the multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol gives
(5p​)=(7p​)=−1.
(57)
Conversely, suppose the two displayed Legendre symbols have the same sign. By quadratic reciprocity,
(p−35​)=(5p​)(7p​)=1.
(58)
Choose an odd integer B satisfying B2≡−35(modp). Since B is odd, B2+35 is also divisible by 4, so
F=[p,B,4pB2+35​]
(59)
is a positive definite integral form of discriminant −35 that represents p. Reducing F yields either f1​ or f2​, and equivalence preserves represented integers. The necessary symbol calculation above determines which one: the positive pair selects f1​, and the negative pair selects f2​. Therefore
p is represented by fi​⟺(5p​)=(7p​)={+1,−1,​i=1,i=2.​​
(60)

The pumping lemma for regular languages states that for every regular language L there is an integer N such that every w∈L with ∣w∣≥N can be written
w=xyz
(61)
with
∣xy∣≤N,∣y∣≥1,xyrz∈Lfor every r≥0.
(62)
To prove it, let a deterministic finite automaton with N states recognize L. During the reading of the first N symbols of an accepted word w, the automaton visits N+1 states, including the initial state. By the pigeonhole principle, two of them agree, say qi​=qj​ with 0≤i<j≤N. Let x be the first i symbols, y the next j−i symbols, and z the remaining suffix. Reading y is a nonempty closed path from qi​ to itself. Traversing this path any number r≥0 of times and then reading z therefore reaches the same accept state. This proves all three assertions.

Solution

Suppose a path took p to a state q. Part (i) implies that no accept state is reachable from either p or q. Thus every possible continuation is rejected from both states, so p and q are indistinguishable states of a deterministic finite automaton. Distinct indistinguishable states cannot occur in a minimal deterministic finite automaton. Therefore q=p, and there is no path from p to any other state.
Equivalently, a cycle state in a minimal deterministic finite automaton for a finite language is the unique rejecting sink.

16G (Logic and Set Theory)

Words: 407 Articles: 9
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 211
16G OurBigBook.com
The compactness theorem for first-order logic says that a set T of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of T has a model. The forward implication is immediate. Conversely, if every finite subset is satisfiable, then T is syntactically consistent: any proof of a contradiction would use only finitely many premises. The Godel completeness theorem then gives a model of T.
The Upward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that a first-order theory with an infinite model has arbitrarily large models. Given an infinite model of T and any cardinal κ, enlarge the language by constants cα​ for α<κ and add
cα​=cβ​(α=β).
(101)
Every finite subset can interpret its finitely many constants as distinct elements of the original infinite model. By the compactness theorem, the enlarged theory has a model containing at least κ distinct elements; its reduct is a model of T.
Finally, suppose a set S and a finite set T axiomatize the same class. Let τ be the conjunction of the sentences in T. Since S⊨τ, the set S∪{¬τ} is unsatisfiable. Compactness gives a finite S0​⊆S such that S0​⊨τ. Because τ⊨S, we also have S0​⊨S, while S⊨S0​ is immediate. Therefore yes: the finite subset S0​ axiomatizes the same theory. This is finite subaxiomatization from an equivalent finite theory.

This is the group instance of the fact that finite structures are not first-order axiomatizable.

Words: 336 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 336
17I OurBigBook.com
A k-colouring assigns one of k colours to every vertex so that adjacent vertices have different colours. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least such k. An independent set contains no adjacent pair, and the independence number α(G) is the maximum size of such a set.
For a concrete first example, start with the five-cycle C5​ and apply the Mycielski construction r−2 times. Each application raises the chromatic number by one and preserves triangle-freeness. The resulting graph has chromatic number r+1>r and contains no triangle, hence no complete graph Kr​ for r≥3.
We next prove the stronger high-girth assertion by the probabilistic method. For a large integer n, take
G∼G(n,p),p=n−1+1/(2g).
(105)
If X counts cycles of lengths 3,…,g, then
EX≤∑j=3g​2jnjpj​=O((np)g)=O(n1/2).
(106)
By the first moment method, with probability tending to one X<n/2.
Let m=⌊n/(2k)⌋. The expected number of independent sets of size m is at most
(mn​)(1−p)(2m​)≤(men​)mexp(−2pm(m−1)​)⟶0,
(107)
because pm2=Θ(n1+1/(2g)) dominates mlog(en/m)=O(n). Hence with positive probability G has fewer than n/2 short cycles and α(G)<m.
Delete one vertex from each cycle of length at most g. The remaining graph H has no such cycle, has at least n/2 vertices, and still has α(H)<n/(2k). Since each colour class is independent,
χ(H)≥α(H)∣V(H)∣​≥k.​
(108)
This proves that there are graphs of arbitrarily high girth and chromatic number.
For the final claim, begin instead with
G∼G(N,p),N=2n,p=N−0.69.
(109)
The expected number T of triangles is
ET=(3N​)p3=O(N0.93)=o(n),
(110)
so with probability tending to one T<n. Put m=⌈n0.7⌉. The expected number of independent m-sets is bounded by
(mN​)(1−p)(2m​)≤exp(mlogmeN​−2pm(m−1)​)⟶0,
(111)
because the positive term is O(n0.7logn) whereas the negative term has order n0.71.
Thus some such G has fewer than n triangles and no independent set of size m. Delete one vertex from every triangle; more than n vertices remain and the graph is triangle-free. Take any induced subgraph on exactly n vertices. Vertex deletion cannot increase the independence number, so the resulting graph satisfies
α(G)<n0.7.​
(112)
This is the triangle-free graph with sub-power independence number construction.

ωχ​(C)=χ(1)∣C∣χ(c)​.

If a degree p occurred, its square would already consume the entire sum p2, leaving no room for the trivial character. Hence every irreducible degree is one. A finite group has only linear irreducible characters exactly when it is abelian, so every group of order p2 is abelian.

Let a be the number of linear characters and b the number of degree-two characters. The linear characters are precisely the characters of the abelianization, so
a=∣G/G′∣∣2p.

The degree-sum formula gives
a+4b=2p,

so a≡2(mod4). Among the divisors of 2p, this forces a=2 or a=2p. In the latter case b=0 and all degrees are one. In the former,
b=42p−2​=2p−1​.

Thus the degrees are
1,1,(p−1)/22,…,2​​​

Suppose a finite simple group had an irreducible representation ρ of degree two. Its kernel is normal and cannot be the whole group, so ρ is faithful. A nonabelian simple group has no nontrivial linear character; consequently detρ is trivial and ρ(G)⊆SL2​(C).
Since 2∣∣G∣ by degree divisibility, Cauchy's theorem for finite groups gives an involution x∈G. A nonidentity matrix of order two in SL2​(C) has both eigenvalues −1, hence equals −I. Thus ρ(x)=−I is central in ρ(G). Faithfulness makes x central in G, contradicting the trivial centre of a nonabelian simple group. Therefore no finite simple group has an irreducible character of degree two.

q∣p−1.​

Because G/P is abelian, the commutator subgroup G′ lies in P. It is nontrivial because G is nonabelian, and ∣P∣=p is prime, so G′=P. Therefore
∣G/G′∣=q,

Every nonlinear irreducible degree divides pq. Its square is at most pq, so the only possibility is degree q. If there are b such characters, the sum of squares of irreducible degrees gives

k(G)=q+qp−1​.​
(138)
These are the irreducible characters of a nonabelian group of order p q.

If Xn​ were homotopy equivalent to a compact connected surface S, the subgroup corresponding to this cover would produce a connected four-sheeted cover S homotopy equivalent to Xn​. Hence Xn​ is not homotopy equivalent to a compact connected surface for any n≥1.

Near the upper turning point, put z=zm​−ζ. Expansion gives
(dxdz​)2≃4aβ2zm​ζ.
(348)
If x=xm​ at the turn, integration yields the local ray path
z≃zm​−aβ2zm​(x−xm​)2.​
(349)
The ray is tangent to the line z=zm​, turns smoothly, crosses z=0, and repeats symmetrically between −zm​ and zm​. Increasing ϕ decreases zm​, while ϕ↓0 sends the turning level outward.

Let δx2​um​=um−1​−2um​+um+1​. For an exact smooth solution of the diffusion equation, the second-order central difference gives
δx2​u(x,t)=h2uxx​(x,t)+12h4​uxxxx​(x,t)+O(h6).
(350)
Since the Courant number μ=k/h2 is fixed, h2=O(k). Taylor expansion in time gives
u(t+k)−u(t)23​μδx2​u(t)−21​μδx2​u(t−k)​=kut​+2k2​utt​+O(k3),=kuxx​+2k2​uxxt​+O(kh2)+O(k3).​
(351)
Using ut​=uxx​ and utt​=uxxt​ cancels the leading terms. Because kh2=O(k2), the residual, and hence the local truncation error in the convention of the question, is
O(k2).​
(352)

For a discrete Fourier mode umn​=rneimθ, put
q=4μsin22θ​,0≤q≤4μ.
(353)
The recurrence becomes
rn+1=(1−23​q)rn+21​qrn−1,
(354)
so its amplification polynomial of a multilevel finite difference scheme is
p(r)=r2−(1−23​q)r−21​q.
(355)
Its roots are real. Moreover,
p(1)=q,p(−1)=2(1−q),2r1​+r2​​=21​−43​q.
(356)
The root-location criterion in the question therefore puts both roots in [−1,1] exactly when 0≤q≤1. Fourier stability analysis for every wavenumber is equivalent to 4μ≤1, so
the scheme is stable if and only if μ≤41​.​
(357)

For the same Fourier mode, the leapfrog finite-difference scheme for the diffusion equation gives
rn+1=rn−1−2qrn,p(r)=r2+2qr−1.
(358)
The two amplification roots are
r±​=−q±1+q2​.
(359)
For every nonzero mode q>0, one has
∣r−​∣=q+1+q2​>1.
(360)
Thus every μ>0 admits a growing Fourier mode, and
the leapfrog scheme is unstable for every μ>0.​
(361)
